evidence.field: 名 entry; printed p. 81, PDF p. 93; source scan pixel hash 6675f9f0dc70221f985d09414ae5966cd8260c50bf82e1c38830cf5866905834
evidence.text: The visible headword is 名. The entry calls it a semantic compound of 口 and 夕, explaining them through identifying oneself by speaking when people cannot see each other at night. It says the graph occurs in oracle-bone inscriptions, but there for place names or sacrificial names rather than the basic sense. It describes a Spring-and-Autumn bronze use as the basic sense, then gives a naming verb use on the 少虞 sword and describes later extensions from personal names to names of things, status, and reputation. Scan pixels inspected directly; the entry ends on this page. The passage’s unusual graph in the Qin-gong quotation was not used to support these claims.

evidence.text: The visible headword is 夕. The entry says its ancient forms resemble the moon at moonrise; 夕 and 月 were originally one graph and later differentiated. It gives 暮夜 (dusk/night) as the graph’s original sense and cites oracle-bone uses with 夕 meaning evening. Scan pixels inspected directly; no continuation is needed for this passage.

evidence.source: Academia Sinica, Institute of History and Philology, Ancient Chinese Character Database
evidence.field: 名 graphic evolution and component account
evidence.text: The entry lists oracle-bone, bronze (including collection no. 04293), Chu manuscript, small-seal and Shuowen forms. It identifies the upper part as 夕 and the lower part as 口, and presents both as semantic in the night-identification explanation. This records the received interpretation; it does not independently establish that account as the original motivation.
evidence.title: 漢字「名」：字形演變

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.field: 夕 and 名 accounts; cited uses
evidence.text: The 夕 entry says its basic sense is sunset and moonrise, sometimes extending to night, and describes 夕 and 月 as graphically differentiated later. For 名 it repeats the Shuowen night-identification explanation; reports an oracle-bone place-name token 《乙》3290; gives a Western Zhou bronze naming verb on the 少虡 sword; and cites a bronze use glossed as 銘 ‘inscription’ plus Warring States manuscript examples of name/designation uses. These examples attest different uses but do not establish a continuous semantic path or the first dates of the listed senses.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 夕 (includes 名 entry)

evidence.source: English Wiktionary, 名 entry; reconstruction fields attributed there to Baxter–Sagart 2014 and Zhengzhang
evidence.field: alternative graphic analysis and host pronunciation
evidence.text: The page reports a proposal that 口 once wrote both 口 and 名, and that 夕—interpreted there as standing for a graph later written 明—was added as a phonetic indicator. The page does not supply a primary paleographic argument for this proposal. It lists 名 as Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese *C.meŋ and Zhengzhang Old Chinese *meŋ; those host readings alone do not establish a phonetic role for 夕.
evidence.title: 名 — Wiktionary

evidence.source: English Wiktionary, 夕 entry; reconstruction fields attributed there to Baxter–Sagart 2014 and Zhengzhang
evidence.text: The page lists 夕 as Mandarin xī, Middle Chinese zjek, Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese *s-ɢAk and Zhengzhang Old Chinese *ljaːɡ. Compared within Baxter–Sagart notation, 夕 *s-ɢAk differs substantially from 名 *C.meŋ; this does not support the reported 夕-as-phonetic proposal under that reconstruction. These character readings do not determine the ancient identity or function of the proposed graphic component.
evidence.title: 夕 — 维基词典

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The entry records the Shuowen analysis of 名 as 从口从夕 and its night-identification explanation. It lists personal name, naming, names of things, written characters, status, reputation and other senses, but the list does not date their emergence.

search_audit.outcome: Search returned repeated conventional accounts and the secondary alternative. No primary study adjudicating the alternative was found in these results.

Local corpus search located the 名 headword on PDF page 93 and the separate 夕 entry on PDF page 635. Both supplied scan images were opened and inspected directly; 名 is printed p. 81 and 夕 p. 622. The relevant cited prose was legible and no OCR correction was needed for the claims recorded.

gaps: The reported 夕-as-phonetic analysis, including its proposed connection to a graph later written 明, remains a secondary proposal without a primary paleographic defense located in this search. The inspected Baxter–Sagart readings for 名 and 夕 differ substantially, but pronunciation comparison alone does not adjudicate an early graphic analysis.

字源 identifies the earliest oracle-bone uses as place names or sacrificial names, while the inspected CUHK entry specifically reports a place-name token. The token’s date and precise interpretation remain unresolved.

Attestations and lexicographic lists do not establish first dates or a continuous semantic path among personal name, naming, inscription, reputation and status uses. 字源’s attribution of a Spring-and-Autumn bronze use to the basic sense is an inspected source interpretation, not by itself a dated first-occurrence proof.

The supplied local scan passage includes an unusual graph with a parenthetical reading in its Qin-gong quotation. Its exact Unicode identity was not needed for the paraphrases here and was not adopted as evidence.

Unicode’s character-specific U+540D and U+5915 record pages returned internal errors. The checkout also lacks the full local Unihan_Readings.txt and baxtersagart.tsv sources referenced in the dossier, so local-row rechecking and official Unihan click-through verification remain incomplete.
